item.title: Identity and Security
item.description:
Organizations are the basic unit of multi-tenancy inside of Layer5 Cloud. The identity structure is highly flexible: organizations can have any number of teams, teams can have any number of users, and users can belong to any number of teams and organizations.

Below is an overview of the core identity components within the Layer5 Cloud.

Identity 🔗

Organizations serve as the fundamental component of multi-tenancy within the Layer5 Cloud.

item.title: Roles
item.description:
A role is the unit you assign to people. It answers the question “what is this person here to do?” and translates that answer into permissions. Layer5 Cloud builds every role from the same three layers:

  • A key allows exactly one action, such as creating a team or approving a catalog request. See Keys.
  • A keychain bundles related keys, such as everything needed to manage teams. See Keychains.
  • A role bundles keychains.

A user’s permissions in an organization are the union of the keys from every role they hold in that organization. Holding two roles never removes anything; it only adds. The organization in context decides which roles count: the same person can administer one organization and hold only the User role in another, and their permissions differ accordingly. When a request names an organization, that organization is the context, even if the session points at a different one. Security Boundaries explains why the organization is an authorization boundary.

item.title: Permissions by Role
item.description:
This page tells you which Kanvas actions require a permission, which default roles grant each permission, and which actions are limited by something other than a permission. Use it to find out why an action is missing for a user and which role grants it.

How permissions work 🔗

A permission is a named key, such as Deploy Design, that allows one action. Keys are grouped into keychains, and a role bundles one or more keychains. Your organization assigns roles to users. Before Kanvas offers certain actions, it checks whether the user holds the matching key. Kanvas uses the shared Layer5 permission set and defines no permissions of its own. See Roles and Keychains.

item.title: Roles and Permissions
item.description:
This page tells you which permissions each default Layer5 Cloud role holds. Use it to find out why an action is missing for a user and which role grants it. For how roles, keychains, and permissions fit together, see Roles.

How permission checks work 🔗

A permission is a named key that allows one action, such as Create Team. A keychain groups keys, and a role groups keychains. Layer5 Cloud checks the key, never the role name. Before it runs a guarded action, Cloud resolves the organization the request names, then checks whether the user holds the key through a role in that organization. A user’s permissions are the union of the keys from every role the user holds there.

item.title: Build a Custom Keychain
item.description:
A custom keychain bundles the keys that a custom role needs. This guide creates a keychain, changes its keys, and deletes it. It is written for Provider Admins and self-hosted operators, because only they can complete the whole path from keys to users. For the model, read the Keychains concept.

Before you start 🔗

  • You need the Create Keychain, Edit Keychain, and Delete Keychain permissions to use the matching controls. Provider Admin holds all three. No other default role does.
  • A keychain does nothing until a role includes it. Creating and editing roles is a Provider Admin action. On hosted Layer5 Cloud an organization cannot complete this path alone. On a self-hosted deployment, your Provider Admins can.
  • Keychains are not organization-scoped. A role that includes your keychain grants its keys to every user who holds that role, in every organization.

Create a keychain 🔗

Open the Keychains tab under Security and create a keychain. Give it a name and choose the keys it bundles. Layer5 Cloud creates the keychain and adds each key to it. If adding a key fails, the interface reports it as “Failed to add key to keychain”. Open the keychain and confirm every key you chose is present.

item.title: Keys
item.description:
A key is a named permission for exactly one action, such as Create Organization, Approve Catalog Request, or Download Token. Every authorization decision in Layer5 Cloud comes down to one question: does this user hold the key this action requires, in this organization? Understanding keys tells you why a user can or cannot do something, and whether the model fits the access rules you need.

How a key reaches a user 🔗

Keys roll up in three layers. A keychain groups related keys, a role groups keychains, and a user holds roles in an organization or a team. A user never receives a key directly: granting a key means placing it in a keychain that belongs to a role the user holds.

item.title: Keychains
item.description:
A keychain is a named bundle of keys. It sits between the single permission and the role a person holds:

  • A key allows one action, such as Create Token.
  • A keychain groups related keys, such as everything needed to manage teams.
  • A role groups keychains, and users hold roles in an organization or team.

A user’s effective keys in an organization are the union of the keys in every keychain of every role the user holds there. A keychain grants nothing by itself. It takes effect only through a role that includes it.

item.title: Sessions
item.description:
A session is the credential Layer5 Cloud issues each time someone signs in. It is what keeps a browser tab, a second device, or a connected Meshery Server signed in, and it is what you end when you want one of those sign-ins to stop working. Sessions expire on their own; API tokens do not.

One session per sign-in 🔗

Every sign-in creates its own session. Each browser, device, and Meshery Server that signs in through Layer5 Cloud holds a separate session with its own expiry, and any number of them can be active at once. Ending one session leaves the others untouched.
